title: Hip Pain (Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome)
patient_instructions: You are Jay Whitfield, a 58-year-old office worker (or retiree). For about 6 weeks you have had a nagging pain on the OUTER (lateral) side of your RIGHT hip. If asked to point, you place your hand over the bony prominence on the side of the hip, not the groin. The pain is a dull ache, about 5/10, worse when you climb stairs, get out of the car, or walk your dog, and it is worst when you lie on that side in bed at night so your sleep is disturbed. It is a bit better with rest. You have NOT had any fall or injury. You do NOT have fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, lumps, or a chronic cough. You have NOT had steroids, do not drink heavily (2 standard drinks on weekends), have never dislocated or fractured the hip. No groin pain, no locking, no back pain, no pins and needles or leg weakness, no urinary or bowel symptoms, no calf pain on walking. If the doctor offers pain relief, accept politely. Your IDEAS: you are worried you might be 'getting arthritis like my mother'. Your CONCERNS: that it could be something serious or that you will need a hip replacement. Your EXPECTATIONS: you want to know what it is and what can be done so you can sleep. Affect: cooperative, slightly anxious, gives extra detail only when asked.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Jay Whitfield, aged 58, presents with several weeks of right hip pain. Tasks: (1) Take a focused history over approximately 6 minutes, clarifying what 'hip pain' means and systematically excluding joint, referred, neurological, vascular and red-flag causes. (2) Explain your most likely diagnosis and your key differentials to the patient in plain language, giving your reasons. You are not required to examine the patient. Marks are awarded for a structured pain assessment, screening for must-not-miss causes, and a clear patient-centred explanation.
examiner_instructions: The candidate should localise the pain to the LATERAL hip (greater trochanter), elicit the discriminating features (worse lying on that side at night, worse on stairs/rising, no groin pain, no trauma) and reach a working diagnosis of greater trochanteric pain syndrome (gluteus medius tendinopathy / trochanteric bursitis). Reward a Murtagh-style grouped differential: true joint pathology felt in the GROIN and reproduced by internal rotation (OA, avascular necrosis) versus lateral GTPS. Candidates must actively screen red flags: fracture (unable to weight-bear after a fall), septic arthritis/osteomyelitis (fever), malignancy/metastasis (rest/night pain, weight loss), and vascular buttock claudication. Note: statins are NOT an avascular-necrosis risk factor; do not reward that question. If asked, confirm the patient has no fever, weight loss or trauma. Use the rubric; prompt only once if the candidate stalls: 'Anything else you want to ask about?'

criteria: Structured pain assessment (site, onset, character, radiation, aggravating/relieving, severity, night pain)
Clarifies what 'hip pain' means and localises to lateral hip vs groin vs back
Screens joint, soft-tissue/neuro, referred and vascular groups
States greater trochanteric pain syndrome as most likely with reasons (lateral pain, worse lying on side)
Gives relevant differentials: hip OA (groin, internal rotation), avascular necrosis, lumbar radiculopathy, referred pain
Actively screens and safety-nets red flags (fracture, septic arthritis, malignancy, vascular claudication)
Outlines first-line management: activity modification, paracetamol first-line, targeted gluteal physiotherapy, weight optimisation, corticosteroid injection if refractory; imaging only if unclear
Explains diagnosis in plain language, explores ICE
Empathy, checks understanding, safety-nets return advice

red_flags: Inability to weight-bear after a fall (hip/femoral neck fracture) - requires urgent X-ray
Fever with severe hip pain (septic arthritis / osteomyelitis) - urgent referral, potentially 000
Rest pain, night pain and unexplained weight loss (metastatic bone disease / malignancy)
Buttock/leg pain reliably brought on by walking and relieved by rest (vascular claudication)
australian_guidelines: John Murtagh General Practice 8th Ed (Hip and buttock pain, p.1543): in a middle-aged/elderly patient with 'hip pain' consider the under-diagnosed greater trochanteric pain syndrome; use the diagnostic strategy model to exclude serious causes (buttock claudication, metastatic cancer)

eTG / RACGP first-line musculoskeletal analgesia: paracetamol first-line, short course NSAID if suitable and not contraindicated, with load/activity modification and physiotherapy for gluteal tendinopathy
AMC Handbook of Clinical Assessment: station assesses clinical reasoning, examination/investigational planning and diagnostic/management pathways
learning_objectives: Apply the Murtagh 'true hip vs referred' framework to localise hip pain
Distinguish lateral GTPS from groin-based joint pathology using history
Systematically screen must-not-miss causes of hip pain
Outline Australian first-line management of GTPS
key_points: True joint pathology (OA, AVN) is felt in the GROIN and reproduced by internal rotation; GTPS gives LATERAL point tenderness and pain lying on that side
Worse lying on the affected side at night and on rising/stairs is the classic GTPS pattern
Statins are NOT an established avascular-necrosis risk factor; corticosteroids and alcohol are
A negative screen for fever, weight loss and trauma is what allows GTPS to remain the top diagnosis

citations.claim: In a middle-aged/elderly patient with 'hip pain', greater trochanteric pain syndrome is a commonly under-diagnosed cause; the diagnostic strategy model also lists referred spinal pain, OA and serious causes (buttock claudication, metastatic cancer).
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1543

citations.claim: The AMC assessment blueprint covers clinical reasoning, examination/investigational skills and planning diagnostic/management pathways, anchoring the station's structured approach.
citations.source: AMC Handbook of Clinical Assessment.pdf, p.1

citations.claim: Red-flag pointers for musculoskeletal pain include fever (septic arthritis/osteomyelitis) and skin redness/swelling, supporting the infection screen.
